questions.stem:
Consider a stack $S$ and a queue $Q$. Both of them are initially empty and have the capacity to store ten elements each. The elements 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 arrive one by one, in that order. When an element arrives, it is assigned either to $S$ (pushed on $S$) or to $Q$ (enqueued to $Q$). Once all the five elements are stored, the output is generated in two steps. First, stack $S$ is emptied by popping all elements. Then queue $Q$ is emptied by dequeueing all elements. The output obtained by following this process is 4 3 1 2 5.

Given the output, the objective is to predict whether an element was assigned to $S$ or $Q$.

Which of the following options is/are possible valid assignment(s) of the elements?

Note: In the options, the notation $xS$ denotes that element $x$ was assigned to $S$ and $yQ$ denotes that element $y$ was assigned to $Q$.

solutionDiagram.alt: For each of the four options, the five boxes show which element went to the stack (solid) or the queue (dashed), then the stack bottom to top, the queue front to back, and the output; options A and B give 4 3 1 2 5, options C and D give 5 4 1 2 3 and 3 2 1 4 5.

steps.title: The two containers and the rule that decides the output
steps.body: A stack is last in, first out: pop returns the element pushed most recently, so a stack that received some elements returns them in the reverse of their arrival order. A queue is first in, first out: dequeue returns the element enqueued earliest, so a queue returns its elements in arrival order. Elements arrive in the order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and each one goes to $S$ or to $Q$. The output is the stack emptied first and the queue emptied next. So the output is: the elements assigned to $S$ in decreasing order, followed by the elements assigned to $Q$ in increasing order. A valid output is therefore a decreasing run followed by an increasing run, and the cut between the two runs tells us which elements went where.
steps.tex: \text{output} = \underbrace{S\text{-elements, largest first}}_{\text{stack pops}} \;\Big|\; \underbrace{Q\text{-elements, smallest first}}_{\text{queue dequeues}}

steps.title: Cut the target 4 3 1 2 5 into a decreasing run and an increasing run
steps.body: Try each place to cut 4 3 1 2 5. The first part must be decreasing and the second part increasing. Cut after 4: the second part 3 1 2 5 is not increasing (3 then 1). Cut after 4 3: first part 4 3 is decreasing, second part 1 2 5 is increasing, so this works. Cut after 4 3 1: first part 4 3 1 is decreasing, second part 2 5 is increasing, so this works as well. Cut after 4 3 1 2: first part is not decreasing (1 then 2). Cut at the very start (empty stack) needs 4 3 1 2 5 increasing, and cutting at the very end needs it decreasing; both fail. So exactly two cuts survive. Element 1 is the one that is free: it can sit at the bottom of the stack (popped last from the stack) or at the front of the queue (dequeued first), and both put 1 right after 3 in the output.

steps.title: Turn each cut into an assignment and compare with the options
steps.body: Cut 4 3 1 | 2 5 gives $S = \{1, 3, 4\}$ and $Q = \{2, 5\}$, which is 1S, 2Q, 3S, 4S, 5Q: option (A). Cut 4 3 | 1 2 5 gives $S = \{3, 4\}$ and $Q = \{1, 2, 5\}$, which is 1Q, 2Q, 3S, 4S, 5Q: option (B). Option (C) puts 4 and 5 in $S$: 5 was pushed after 4, so the first pop is 5, and the output would begin with 5 instead of 4. Option (D) puts 1, 2, 3 in $S$: the first pop is 3, so the output begins with 3 instead of 4. A script tried all 32 ways of assigning five elements and found exactly two that produce 4 3 1 2 5, the assignments of (A) and (B). The answer is (A) and (B).

shortcut.body: Look at the first output number. It is the last element pushed on $S$, or the front of $Q$ if $S$ is empty. Here 4 comes first, so 4 is the most recent element in $S$, which means 5 was not pushed on $S$ after it: 5 must be in $Q$. That removes (C), where 5S. In (D) the stack holds 1, 2, 3 and the first pop is 3, not 4. Check (A) and (B) by writing the output: stack part read from the top, then the queue part. Both give 4 3 1 2 5. About 90 seconds. Do not stop after finding one correct option; in an MSQ the second cut (element 1 in the queue instead of the stack) is the usual miss.

traps.text: Option (A) is correct, but a candidate who finds 4 3 1 | 2 5 and stops misses option (B). The cut between the decreasing run and the increasing run is not unique when the element after the run's end can extend either run.
Option (B) is correct and is the one people leave out: element 1 can be the front of the queue instead of the bottom of the stack, because 1 sits between 3 and 2 in the output either way.
Option (C) puts 4 and 5 on the stack. Candidates see 4 in the stack and forget that 5 arrives later and lands above it, so 5 would be popped first and the output would start with 5.
Option (D) puts 1, 2, 3 on the stack and 4, 5 on the queue. The stack returns 3 2 1 and the queue 4 5, giving 3 2 1 4 5. Reading 'stack first' as 'smallest elements first' is the slip.

recognize.clues: A stack and a queue are emptied one after the other, and the question gives the final output and asks which element-to-container assignments could have produced it. The word "possible" with several options marks it as a multiple-select check.
recognize.contrast: The classic stack-permutation question lets pushes and pops interleave on a single stack. Here every push is done before any pop, so there is nothing to interleave; the output is just a falling run followed by a rising run.

check.body: Boundary check: putting all five elements in Q gives 1 2 3 4 5 and putting all five in S gives 5 4 3 2 1, and neither equals the target, so the split must lie strictly inside. Then substitute: for each option write its S elements in descending order, then its Q elements in ascending order, and compare with 4 3 1 2 5 position by position.

questions.stem:
Consider the following code snippet in C language that computes the number of nodes in a non-empty singly linked list pointed to by the pointer variable $head$.

Which one of the following options gives the correct replacements for the expressions E1 and E2?

solutionDiagram.alt: A three-node list n1, n2, n3 followed by NULL. Under option B the calls return 3, 2, 1 for n1, n2, n3; under option C the calls return 4, 3, 2 and the call on NULL returns 1, so the count is one too many.

steps.title: What a singly linked list is, and how recursion measures its length
steps.body: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value (elt) and a pointer next to the following node, and the last node's next is NULL. A pointer head names the first node. Recursion measures the list by this rule: the length of the list starting at a node is 1 (the node itself) plus the length of the list that starts at its next node. A recursive function needs two parts. The base case answers the smallest problem directly, without calling itself. The recursive case calls itself on a strictly smaller problem, here the list starting at head->next. The question promises the list is non-empty, so head is never NULL on the first call.

steps.title: The recursive call must move to the next node
steps.body: E2 is returned when E1 is false, and it must add this node's 1 to the size of the rest. The rest of the list starts at head->next. So E2 is 1 + getListSize(head->next). Options (A) and (D) write 1 + getListSize(head): the same pointer is passed again, the list never gets shorter, and the calls never end (stack overflow). They are wrong whatever E1 is.

steps.title: The base case must stop at the last node, not after it
steps.body: The smallest non-empty list is one node, recognised by head->next == NULL, and its size is 1: that is exactly what 'if (E1) return 1' returns. Option (C) tests head == NULL instead. That test is only true after the recursion has stepped past the last node, and then it returns 1 for a node that does not exist, so every list is counted one too long. Check on three nodes n1, n2, n3 with option (B): getListSize(n3) sees n3->next == NULL and returns 1; getListSize(n2) returns 1 + 1 = 2; getListSize(n1) returns 1 + 2 = 3. With option (C) the call on NULL returns 1, and the totals become 2, 3, 4: the answer 4 for a 3-node list. A script confirmed this: (B) returns n for lists of 1 to 5 nodes, (C) returns n + 1, and (A) and (D) recurse without end. The answer is (B).

shortcut.body: Throw out (A) and (D) first: they pass head again, so the problem never shrinks. Between (B) and (C), test the smallest legal input, a one-node list. (B): head->next is NULL, return 1, correct. (C): head is not NULL, so it returns 1 + getListSize(NULL) = 1 + 1 = 2, wrong. About 30 seconds. The one-node test is safe because the question says the list is non-empty.

traps.text: Option (A) combines the wrong base case with a call that does not advance. It never terminates on any list, because head is never NULL on the first call and the same pointer is passed again.

Option (C) is the pattern from textbooks where the empty list has size 0 and the base case is head == NULL. Here the base case returns 1, so the empty-list base case counts a phantom node and the result is one too large.

Option (D) has the right base case but does not advance. It happens to work on a one-node list, which makes it look correct on a quick test, and then fails on every longer list by recursing on the same node forever.

recognize.clues: A node struct with a next pointer, a function that returns the size of a non-empty list, and two blanks that must be the base case and the recursive step.
recognize.contrast: For lists that may be empty the usual base case is head == NULL returning 0. This question promises a non-empty list and returns 1, so the base case must recognise the last node instead, which changes both blanks.

check.body: Trace a two-node list n1 -> n2 call by call: the top call must return 2, and no call may dereference NULL. Also count the calls: a correct version makes exactly one call per node, so for a list of length $n$ the call count equals $n$.

The first option calls on head again and never ends. The second tests head == NULL, so it reads head->elt through a NULL pointer after the last node. questions.stem:
Consider a stack data structure into which we can PUSH and POP records. Assume that each record pushed in the stack has a positive integer key and that all keys are distinct.

We wish to augment the stack data structure with an $O(1)$ time MIN operation that returns a pointer to the record with smallest key present in the stack

1) without deleting the corresponding record, and
2) without increasing the complexities of the standard stack operations.

Which one or more of the following approach(es) can achieve it?
options: Keep with every record in the stack, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it.
Keep a pointer to the record with the smallest key in the stack.
Keep an auxiliary array in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained in sorted order.
Keep a Min-Heap in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two stacks of records. After pushing keys 5, 3, 7, 2 the records store below_min = none, 5, 3, 3 (the smallest key strictly below each); MIN compares the top key 2 with its below_min 3 and gives 2. After popping the key 2 the top record 7 stores below_min 3, so MIN is 3.

steps.title: What is being asked, and the real difficulty
steps.body: A stack is last in, first out. PUSH puts a record on top and POP removes the top record; both take $O(1)$ time. We want a third operation MIN that returns a pointer to the record with the smallest key currently inside the stack, also in $O(1)$, while PUSH and POP stay $O(1)$. The smallest key changes in two ways. A new record may be smaller than everything (easy to notice at PUSH time). Worse, when the current minimum is popped, the new minimum is the smallest of the records that remain, and it must be found in $O(1)$ at that moment. So the information 'what is the minimum of everything below me' has to be saved earlier, at PUSH time, for every position. The test for each option: can PUSH, POP and MIN all stay $O(1)$?

steps.title: Option (A): store with each record the pointer to the smallest record below it
steps.body: Give every record a field below_min that points to the smallest-key record among the records under it (NULL for the bottom record). MIN returns whichever of the top record and top->below_min has the smaller key: one comparison, $O(1)$. PUSH of a new record r looks at the old top t and sets r->below_min to the smaller of t and t->below_min: one comparison, $O(1)$. POP removes the top; every record that stays has a below_min that points only to records beneath it, so none is stale, and nothing needs repair: $O(1)$. This works, and it is the standard min-stack. After pushing 5, 3, 7, 2, the records hold below_min = none, 5, 3, 3, so MIN is 2; after one POP the top is 7 with below_min 3, so MIN is 3.

steps.title: Option (B): one pointer to the current minimum fails on POP
steps.body: A single pointer to the smallest record is correct until the minimum itself is popped. Push 5, then 3, then 2: the pointer points to 2. POP removes 2, and the true minimum is now 3, but the single pointer has no way to name it. Finding it means scanning the remaining records, $O(n)$, which increases the cost of POP (or MIN). A script that pops from [5, 3, 2] shows the pointer still naming the popped record while the true minimum is 3. Option (B) fails.

steps.title: Options (C) and (D): ordered structures make PUSH and POP too slow
steps.body: Option (C) keeps the keys of the stack in a sorted auxiliary array. MIN is the first cell, $O(1)$. But PUSH must insert the new key at its sorted position; even if binary search finds the place in $O(\log n)$, the later entries must shift one cell each, $O(n)$ in the worst case. POP likewise removes a key from the middle of the array. Option (D) keeps a min-heap. Reading the smallest key is $O(1)$, but inserting a key costs $O(\log n)$, and a POP of the stack top removes an arbitrary heap entry (the top record is rarely the heap's minimum), which also costs $O(\log n)$. Both options raise the complexity of PUSH and POP, which condition 2 forbids. Only (A) satisfies both conditions, so the answer is (A) alone.

shortcut.body: O(1) MIN under POP means the answer to 'what is the minimum after this record leaves' must already be stored with the records. Ask of each option: does it store one value per position, filled at PUSH time? Only (A) does. (B) stores one value for the whole stack, and (C) and (D) are ordered structures, whose insertion is never $O(1)$. About 60 seconds. This shortcut relies on the usual cost of heaps and sorted arrays and would not apply to a structure with $O(1)$ insertion.

traps.text: Option (B) works until the minimum is popped, and candidates test it only with pushes. The failure appears at POP: the next smallest key is not recorded anywhere, so recovering it takes a scan.
Option (C) has an $O(1)$ MIN, which is the part the question highlights, but PUSH needs a sorted insertion that shifts entries, so PUSH becomes $O(n)$ and condition 2 breaks.

Option (D) is attractive because a heap's find-min is $O(1)$. Its insert is $O(\log n)$ and removing the popped record from the middle of the heap is $O(\log n)$ too, so the standard stack operations get slower.

recognize.clues: A stack is being augmented with an extra O(1) operation while PUSH and POP keep their cost, and the question says "one or more" so every approach must be tested on its own.
recognize.contrast: A min-heap also gives the minimum in O(1), but it is a priority queue: removing the stack top deletes an arbitrary heap entry. Tell them apart by asking which record the next POP must remove: the newest one, not the smallest.

check.body: Run the chosen design on push 4, 9, 2, 7 and then pop twice. MIN must read 2 after the pushes, 2 after the first pop and 4 after the second. A design that can only reproduce this by scanning the remaining records does not meet the O(1) requirement.

We want an O(1) MAX operation that returns a pointer to the record with the largest key present, without deleting it and without increasing the complexity of PUSH and POP. Which one or more of the following approaches achieve it?
options: Keep with every record a pointer to the record with the largest key among itself and the records below it.
Keep a single pointer to the record with the largest key in the stack, updated on every PUSH.
Keep the records of the stack in a sorted linked list, largest key first.
Keep a second stack that receives a key at PUSH time if that stack is empty or the key exceeds its top, and pop it when the popped record equals its top.
variation.explanation: The largest key that remains after a POP has to be stored before the POP happens. The first option stores it per record and the last stores it in a helper stack, so both keep every operation at O(1); random tests of 400 push and pop runs agreed with the true maximum for both. The single pointer goes wrong as soon as the maximum is popped, and a sorted list needs a walk of up to $n$ nodes to insert.

questions.stem:
Let LIST be a datatype for an implementation of linked list defined as follows:

Suppose a program has created two linked lists, L1 and L2, whose contents are given in the figure below (code for creating L1 and L2 is not provided here). L1 contains 9 nodes, and L2 contains 7 nodes.

Consider the following C program segment that modifies the list L1. The number of nodes that will be there in L1 after the execution of the code segment is ________ . (Answer in integer)
questions.figure: Two singly linked lists, each ending in NULL. L1 has 9 nodes holding, from the head: 1, 7, 12, 3, 9, 5, 11, 15, 8. L2 has 7 nodes holding, from the head: 1, 11, 6, 9, 15, 12, 4.

diagram.alt: Two singly linked lists drawn as boxes with arrows: L1 holds 1, 7, 12, 3, 9, 5, 11, 15, 8 and L2 holds 1, 11, 6, 9, 15, 12, 4.

solutionDiagram.alt: L1 drawn with the nodes 12, 9, 11 and 15 marked as present in L2 and unlinked, the first node 1 marked as never tested, and the resulting list 1, 7, 3, 5, 8 below.

steps.title: Linked lists, unlinking, and what the loop examines
steps.body: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes; each node holds data and a pointer next to the following node, and the last next is NULL. L1 and L2 are the pointers to the first nodes. To remove a node X from the chain you do not free-and-shift as in an array; you make the node before X skip it: pred->next = X->next. The loop keeps a pointer ptr1 to a node and always looks one node ahead, at ptr1->next. If the value of that next node occurs in L2 (found by find, a linear search of L2), the next node is unlinked and ptr1 stays where it is. Otherwise ptr1 moves forward. The first node of L1, the one ptr1 points to at the start, is never the 'next' of anything, so it is never tested and never removed, whatever its value.

steps.title: Values of L2, then the walk through L1
steps.body: L2 holds {1, 11, 6, 9, 15, 12, 4}. L1 is 1, 7, 12, 3, 9, 5, 11, 15, 8. Start with ptr1 at 1. Next is 7: not in L2, move ptr1 to 7. Next is 12: in L2, unlink it, so 7 now points to 3 and ptr1 stays at 7. Next is 3: not in L2, move to 3. Next is 9: in L2, unlink, 3 now points to 5. Next is 5: not in L2, move to 5. Next is 11: in L2, unlink, 5 now points to 15 and ptr1 stays. Next is 15: in L2, unlink, 5 now points to 8. Next is 8: not in L2, move to 8. Its next is NULL, so the loop ends. Because ptr1 does not move after an unlink, two matching nodes in a row (11 and 15) are both removed.

steps.title: Count what is left
steps.body: The surviving list is 1, 7, 3, 5, 8: five nodes. As a count: 9 nodes at the start, and four of them (12, 9, 11, 15) were found in L2 and unlinked, so $9 - 4 = 5$. The first node 1 also occurs in L2, but it is never tested. A script that ran the loop on the two lists printed [1, 7, 3, 5, 8], length 5. The answer is 5.

shortcut.body: Cross out every value of L1 that also appears in L2, except the first node: 12, 9, 11, 15 go, which is four. Then $9 - 4 = 5$. About 60 seconds. This is safe because each unlink does not depend on the others; the loop does not skip anything after an unlink.

traps.text: 4: removing the first node 1 as well, which occurs in L2. The loop tests ptr1->next, so the first node is never examined and stays.

6: reading the loop as moving ptr1 forward after every step. If ptr1 advanced after an unlink, the node 15 right after 11 would be skipped and would stay in the list. The code leaves ptr1 where it is, so 15 is also removed.
9: counting L1 as unchanged, or misreading find as a test on L1 instead of L2.

recognize.clues: A while loop that looks one node ahead with ptr1->next->data, an assignment ptr1->next = ptr1->next->next that bypasses a node, and a membership test against a second list.
recognize.contrast: Deleting from an array shifts the later elements; here nothing shifts and the node count drops by one per unlink. A loop that moved ptr1 after every step would skip the node following an unlink, but this one moves only when nothing was removed.

check.body: Count by survivors instead of removals: the first node always stays, and each later node stays only if its value is absent from L2. Walking 7, 12, 3, 9, 5, 11, 15, 8 and keeping those absent from L2 leaves 7, 3, 5, 8, which with the head makes 5 nodes.

variation.stem: A program builds two singly linked lists. L1 has 8 nodes holding, from the head: 9, 2, 9, 9, 4, 7, 2, 5. L2 has 4 nodes holding, from the head: 9, 4, 5, 3. The segment ptr1 = L1; while (ptr1->next != NULL) { query = ptr1->next->data; if (find(query, L2)) ptr1->next = ptr1->next->next; else ptr1 = ptr1->next; } is executed, where find(query, L2) returns 1 if query occurs in L2 and 0 otherwise. The survivors are 9, 2, 7, 2, which is 4 nodes, and a script that ran the loop printed the same list.

questions.stem:
Let S1 and S2 be two stacks. S1 has capacity of 4 elements. S2 has capacity of 2 elements. S1 already has 4 elements: 100, 200, 300, and 400, whereas S2 is empty, as shown below.

Only the following three operations are available:
  PushToS2: Pop the top element from S1 and push it on S2.
  PushToS1: Pop the top element from S2 and push it on S1.
  GenerateOutput: Pop the top element from S1 and output it to the user.

Note that the pop operation is not allowed on an empty stack and the push operation is not allowed on a full stack.

Which of the following output sequences can be generated by using the above operations?
questions.figure: Stack S1 has capacity 4 and holds, from bottom to top, 100, 200, 300, 400, with 400 on top. Stack S2 has capacity 2 and is empty.

diagram.alt: Two stacks drawn as open-top columns: S1 holds 100, 200, 300, 400 with 400 on top and S2 is empty with room for two elements.

solutionDiagram.alt: Tables of the operation sequences for options B, C and D showing S1, S2 and the output after every operation, and a note that option A would need three elements parked in a side stack of two.

steps.title: The machine and the one rule that decides the question
steps.body: A stack lets you touch only its top element. Here S1 starts with 100 at the bottom and 400 on top. Elements leave the machine only through GenerateOutput, which takes the top of S1. S2 is a small side stack, capacity 2, used to park elements. Parking reverses order: if you park 400 and then 300, they come back as 300 first and then 400. The rule: an element can be output only when it is on top of S1, so every element above it must have been parked in S2 or already output; and S2 can hold at most 2 parked elements at any moment. A sequence is possible when some order of the three operations produces it without ever overfilling S2 or S1, and without popping an empty stack.

steps.title: Option (A) 100, 200, 400, 300 is impossible
steps.body: The first output is 100, and 100 is at the bottom of S1. Before it can be output, 200, 300 and 400 must all be off S1 without having been output (they come later in the sequence). They would all have to be parked in S2, but S2 holds only 2. So the first output cannot be 100. A search over every reachable state (a script tried all sequences of the three operations) confirms that no sequence of operations begins with 100.

steps.title: Options (B), (C), (D) each have a working sequence
steps.body:
(B) 200, 300, 400, 100: PushToS2 (400), PushToS2 (300), now 200 is on top, GenerateOutput gives 200. PushToS1 brings 300 back, GenerateOutput gives 300. PushToS1 brings 400 back, GenerateOutput gives 400. GenerateOutput gives 100. S2 reaches its limit of 2 exactly once, which is allowed.
(C) 400, 200, 100, 300: GenerateOutput gives 400. PushToS2 parks 300. GenerateOutput gives 200, GenerateOutput gives 100. PushToS1 brings 300 back, GenerateOutput gives 300.
(D) 300, 200, 400, 100: PushToS2 parks 400. GenerateOutput gives 300, GenerateOutput gives 200. PushToS1 brings 400 back, GenerateOutput gives 400, GenerateOutput gives 100.

shortcut.body: Ask what must be above the first output. Only 400, 300 or 200 can be first: 200 has two elements above it, which S2 can just hold; 100 has three above it, which S2 cannot. About 2 minutes, because each sequence needs its own short run.

traps.text: Option (A) looks harmless because 100, 200 are in order, but starting with 100 means 200, 300 and 400 must all be parked, and the side stack takes only two.
Option (B) is rejected by candidates who think a full side stack is forbidden. A push is forbidden only on a full stack; filling S2 to exactly 2 is allowed, and the third push never happens.
Option (C) is rejected by candidates who think 300 must come out before 200 and 100 because it is above them. It is parked in S2 while they leave and returns afterwards.
Option (D) is rejected by candidates who think 400, being on top, must be the first to leave. Parking 400 lets 300 and 200 leave first, and 400 comes back before 100.

recognize.contrast: The classic stack-permutation question has an input sequence and one stack with unlimited push and pop interleaving. Here the capacity of S2 is what limits the reachable outputs, so test capacity first.

questions.stem:
Let SLLdel be a function that deletes a node in a singly-linked list given a pointer to the node and a pointer to the head of the list. Similarly, let DLLdel be another function that deletes a node in a doubly-linked list given a pointer to the node and a pointer to the head of the list.

Let $n$ denote the number of nodes in each of the linked lists. Which one of the following choices is TRUE about the worst-case time complexity of SLLdel and DLLdel?

solutionDiagram.alt: Top: a singly linked list a, b, c, d, X where three hops from the head reach the predecessor d of the last node X. Bottom: a doubly linked list where the node X is bypassed by two pointer writes through its prev and next links.

steps.title: Deleting a node means fixing the link of the node before it
steps.body: In a singly linked list each node stores only a next pointer, so the chain can be followed in one direction. In a doubly linked list each node stores both next and prev. To delete a node X you must make the node before X (its predecessor) point past X: pred->next = X->next. The whole question is how you find the predecessor when all you hold is a pointer to X (plus the head).

steps.title: Singly linked: the predecessor needs a walk from the head
steps.body: X has no back pointer, so the only way to reach the predecessor is to start at the head and follow next pointers until the node whose next is X. If X is the last node, that is $n - 2$ hops, so the worst case is proportional to $n$. After finding the predecessor the unlinking is two assignments, but the search dominates. SLLdel is $O(n)$ in the worst case.

steps.title: Doubly linked: the predecessor is one step back
steps.body: X->prev is the predecessor, found in one step. Unlinking is X->prev->next = X->next and, when X has a next node, X->next->prev = X->prev; if X is the head the head pointer moves to X->next. Each is a constant number of steps, no walk. DLLdel is $O(1)$. So the statement 'SLLdel is $O(n)$ and DLLdel is $O(1)$' is true: option (D). A script that counted the hops to the predecessor of the last node for lists of 2, 5, 10 and 100 nodes got 0, 3, 8, 98, which is $n - 2$.

shortcut.body: Singly linked plus 'given the node' means a predecessor search, so $O(n)$; doubly linked has the prev pointer, so $O(1)$. That is the reason doubly linked lists exist. About 15 seconds. The 'copy the next node into X and delete the next node' trick gives $O(1)$ for a singly linked list only when X is not the last node, so it does not change the worst case.

traps.text: Option (A) swaps the two lists. It treats the pointer-heavy doubly linked node as the harder one, but the extra prev pointer is exactly what removes the search.
Option (B) has no basis: nothing in an unsorted linked list halves the search, so $\log n$ never appears.

Option (C) is the result of the copy trick: overwrite X with the data of its next node and unlink the next node, which is $O(1)$. It fails when X is the last node (nothing to copy from), and the worst case counts that node.

recognize.clues: Both functions are given a pointer to the node to delete and the head, on a singly linked list and on a doubly linked list, and the question asks for the worst-case time of each.
recognize.contrast: Deleting the node after a given node is O(1) in either list, because the successor is known. Deleting the given node itself needs its predecessor, and only the prev pointer provides that in constant time. Copying the next node into the target does not help when the target is last.

check.body: Boundary case: delete the head. The singly linked version then needs no walk because there is no predecessor, so the linear cost comes from the other end of the list, the last node. For the doubly linked version the head and the last node cost the same constant number of assignments.

questions.stem:
Consider a sequence $a$ of elements $a_0 = 1$, $a_1 = 5$, $a_2 = 7$, $a_3 = 8$, $a_4 = 9$, and $a_5 = 2$. The following operations are performed on a stack $S$ and a queue $Q$, both of which are initially empty.

I: push the elements of $a$ from $a_0$ to $a_5$ in that order into $S$.
II: enqueue the elements of $a$ from $a_0$ to $a_5$ in that order into $Q$.
III: pop an element from $S$.
IV: dequeue an element from $Q$.
V: pop an element from $S$.
VI: dequeue an element from $Q$.
VII: dequeue an element from $Q$ and push the same element into $S$.
VIII: Repeat operation VII three times.
IX: pop an element from $S$.
X: pop an element from $S$.

The top element of $S$ after executing the above operations is ________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Four rows show the stack (bottom to top) and the queue (front to back) after operations I and II, after III to VI, after VII and VIII, and after IX and X; the stack ends as 1, 5, 7, 8, 7, 8 with 8 on top.

steps.title: The two containers: which end each operation uses
steps.body: A stack has one open end, the top: push adds there and pop removes from there, so the last element in is the first out. A queue has two ends: enqueue adds at the back and dequeue removes from the front, so the first element in is the first out. We track the stack bottom to top and the queue front to back, and apply the ten operations in order.

steps.title: Operations I to VI
steps.body: I and II load both containers with 1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 2 in that order. So S (bottom to top) is 1 5 7 8 9 2 with 2 on top, and Q (front to back) is 1 5 7 8 9 2 with 1 at the front. III pops the top of S, which is 2. IV dequeues the front of Q, which is 1. V pops the top of S, which is 9. VI dequeues the front of Q, which is 5. Now S is 1 5 7 8 and Q is 7 8 9 2.

steps.title: Operations VII to X
steps.body: VII moves the front of Q onto S: 7 is dequeued and pushed. 'Repeat operation VII three times' means three more moves, four moves in total, so 8, 9 and 2 follow. The moves empty Q, and S becomes 1 5 7 8 7 8 9 2. IX pops 2 and X pops 9, leaving S = 1 5 7 8 7 8. The top is 8. A script that ran the ten operations printed 8. The answer is 8.

shortcut.body: Only the stack's top matters. Whatever happens to Q, the last four pushes are the queue's remaining elements in order: 7, 8, 9, 2. IX and X remove the last two of them, 2 and 9, so the top is the one pushed just before: 8. About 40 seconds. It depends on first knowing the queue holds 7, 8, 9, 2 after the first two dequeues removed 1 and 5.

traps.text: 2: stopping after the moves from Q and reading the top before IX and X, or forgetting the two final pops.
9: popping once after the moves instead of twice, so 9 is left exposed rather than 8.
7: reading 'Repeat operation VII three times' as three moves in total instead of the original plus three repeats. With only three moves S ends 1 5 7 8 7 8 9, the two pops expose 7.

recognize.clues: Two containers receive the same six values, a mix of pop and dequeue steps follows, a transfer step moves the queue front onto the stack, and the question asks only for the stack top at the end.
recognize.contrast: Popping the stack removes the newest element while dequeuing removes the oldest, and mixing them up gives a wrong top. The words "repeat three times" mean three more moves, so the transfer happens four times in all.

check.body: Size check: the stack has 4 elements after operation VI, gains 4 from the transfers and loses 2 to the last two pops, leaving 6. The top is then the second element moved, the second in the queue order 7 8 9 2 that was transferred.

questions.stem:
Consider the problem of reversing a singly linked list. To take an example, given the linked list below, the reversed linked list should look like the second list in the figure.

Which one of the following statements is TRUE about the time complexity of algorithms that solve the above problem in $O(1)$ space?
questions.figure: A singly linked list: head points to the node a, which points to b, then c, then d, then e, whose next is NULL. The reversed list: head points to e, which points to d, then c, then b, then a, whose next is NULL.

diagram.alt: Two singly linked lists with a head pointer: the original list a, b, c, d, e and the reversed list e, d, c, b, a.

options: The best algorithm for the problem takes $\theta(n)$ time in the worst case.
The best algorithm for the problem takes $\theta(n \log n)$ time in the worst case.
The best algorithm for the problem takes $\theta(n^2)$ time in the worst case.
It is not possible to reverse a singly linked list in $O(1)$ space.

solutionDiagram.alt: Four snapshots of the three-pointer reversal on a, b, c, d, e: at the start, after one step, after two steps and after five steps, with the reversed arrows drawn beneath the nodes and the prev and cur pointers labelled.

steps.title: What 'reverse in O(1) space' means
steps.body: A singly linked list has one pointer per node, next, and a pointer head to the first node. Reversing it means turning every next pointer around, so that the old last node becomes the new first node. Space $O(1)$ means the algorithm uses a fixed number of extra variables, a few pointers, whatever the length $n$ of the list. It may not copy the nodes into an array or a stack, and it may not recurse $n$ deep (the call stack would be $O(n)$ space).

steps.title: An algorithm that runs in O(n) time and O(1) space
steps.body: Keep three pointers: prev (starts NULL), cur (starts at head) and next. Repeat while cur is not NULL: save next = cur->next; turn the pointer around with cur->next = prev; then move prev = cur and cur = next. Each pass handles one node in a constant number of steps, so $n$ nodes take $n$ passes. At the end prev is the old last node, and head is set to it. Extra space is three pointers. So reversal in $O(1)$ space is possible, which already rules out option (D), and its time is $O(n)$.

steps.title: No algorithm can be faster than linear, so the best is Theta(n)
steps.body: Every one of the $n - 1$ links must change direction, and the new head is the old last node, which you can only reach by passing all $n$ nodes. So any algorithm needs at least about $n$ steps: the time is $\Omega(n)$. Together with the $O(n)$ algorithm above, the best worst-case time is $\Theta(n)$. Options (B) and (C) name slower times, so 'the best algorithm takes' them is false. The answer is (A). A script ran the three-pointer loop on lists of 1, 2, 5 and 50 nodes: it returned the reversed list in exactly $n$ passes each time.

shortcut.body: Three-pointer loop: one pass, $n$ nodes, $O(1)$ extra pointers, so $\Theta(n)$ is achievable, and you cannot beat visiting every node. Pick $\theta(n)$. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Option (B) imports the $n \log n$ of sorting. Reversal needs no comparisons, only pointer turns.

Option (C) comes from a naive in-place idea: repeatedly walk to the last node and move it to the front. That is $O(n^2)$ and uses $O(1)$ space, but it is not the best algorithm, and the option talks about the best.
Option (D) comes from knowing that the recursive and stack-based reversals use $O(n)$ space and concluding that reversal needs that much. Turning pointers in place avoids both.

recognize.clues: The task is reversing a singly linked list under a stated space limit of O(1), and the question asks about the best possible worst-case time among four asymptotic classes.
recognize.contrast: Recursive reversal also takes linear time but uses $O(n)$ stack space, and copying the nodes into an array or stack does too. Only in-place pointer reversal meets the O(1) space limit.

check.body: Lower bound: the new head is the old last node, and the only way to find it is to follow next pointers through all $n$ nodes, so fewer than $n$ steps cannot work. Second route: apply the loop twice to a, b, c. The result must be a, b, c again, which holds only if each application turned every link exactly once.

questions.stem: Consider the queues $Q_1$ containing four elements and $Q_2$ containing none (shown as the Initial State in the figure). The only operations allowed on these two queues are Enqueue(Q,element) and Dequeue(Q). The minimum number of Enqueue operations on $Q_1$ required to place the elements of $Q_1$ in $Q_2$ in reverse order (shown as the Final State in the figure) without using any additional storage is ________.
questions.figure: Initial State: queue Q1 holds 1, 2, 3, 4 with its head at the element 1 on the left, and queue Q2 is empty with its head at its left end. Final State: Q1 is empty and Q2 holds 4, 3, 2, 1 with its head at the element 4 on the left.

diagram.alt: Two panels. Initial State: Q1 holds 1, 2, 3, 4 and Q2 is empty, each with its head on the left. Final State: Q1 is empty and Q2 holds 4, 3, 2, 1 from the head.

solutionDiagram.alt: A table of the contents of Q1 and Q2 after each move: four moves from Q1 to Q2 and six rotations of Q2, ending with Q2 as 4, 3, 2, 1 and Q1 empty.

steps.title: Queues, the only two moves, and what is being counted
steps.body: A queue is first in, first out. The head is the end where Dequeue removes an element, and Enqueue adds an element at the other end, the tail. The only moves are Dequeue(Q), which takes the head element out, and Enqueue(Q, x), which puts x at the tail. 'Without any additional storage' means a dequeued element must be enqueued straight away; you cannot hold elements in a variable or array. So each element moves from one queue's head to some queue's tail. The question counts only the Enqueue operations whose target is $Q_1$. Enqueues into $Q_2$ are free.

steps.title: Q2 can reverse itself by rotating
steps.body: Take Dequeue(Q2) followed by Enqueue(Q2, the same element). That moves the head of $Q_2$ to its tail, a rotation, and it is an Enqueue on $Q_2$, so it costs nothing in this count. Rotating a queue $k$ times moves its $k$ front elements behind the rest. So we can build the reversal inside $Q_2$: bring one element from $Q_1$ into $Q_2$ (Dequeue(Q1), Enqueue(Q2, x): again an Enqueue on $Q_2$ only), then rotate $Q_2$ until the newcomer is at the head, ahead of every older element.

steps.title: Run it on 1, 2, 3, 4
steps.body: Q2 after each move, head at the left. Move 1: [1]. Move 2: [1, 2], rotate once: [2, 1]. Move 3: [2, 1, 3], rotate twice: [1, 3, 2], then [3, 2, 1]. Move 4: [3, 2, 1, 4], rotate three times: [2, 1, 4, 3], [1, 4, 3, 2], [4, 3, 2, 1]. This is the Final State: $Q_2$ reads 4, 3, 2, 1 from the head, and $Q_1$ is empty. The operations used are 4 moves plus $0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6$ rotations, 10 Enqueues, all on $Q_2$. Enqueues on $Q_1$: 0. A script that searched all move sequences for the cheapest in Enqueues on $Q_1$ also found 0. Since a count cannot be negative, 0 is the minimum.

shortcut.body: The question counts one kind of Enqueue. If $Q_2$ can do the whole job alone, the answer is 0. $Q_2$ can: after each arrival from $Q_1$, rotate $Q_2$ until the newcomer is at the head. Check the first three arrivals and the pattern is clear. About 90 seconds.

traps.text: 6: assuming the rotations must happen in $Q_1$. To get 4 out first you would dequeue 1, 2, 3 and enqueue them back into $Q_1$ (3 Enqueues), then 2 (for 1, 2), then 1: $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$. That works, but it is not minimal, since $Q_2$ can do the rotating.
10: counting every Enqueue in the whole procedure. The question counts Enqueues on $Q_1$ only, and none of the 10 are on $Q_1$.
4: counting one Enqueue per element moved, forgetting that moving to $Q_2$ is an Enqueue on $Q_2$, not on $Q_1$.

recognize.clues: The question asks only for Enqueue operations on Q1 while the target is a reversal in Q2, with no extra storage. The phrase "only Enqueue and Dequeue" and the count restricted to one queue tell you to see which queue can do the rearranging.
recognize.contrast: A stack reverses by itself with push and pop. A queue cannot, so the reversal needs rotations, and the point is to see that Q2 can rotate itself at no cost to the counted operation, whereas rotating Q1 would be counted.

check.body: Second route: replay the plan for two elements. Move 1, move 2 to give [1, 2], rotate once to give [2, 1]. That is already the reverse, and Q1 was never an Enqueue target. The count of rotations before each arrival is the number of elements already in Q2 minus one, the same pattern as for four elements.

questions.stem: What is the worst case time complexity of inserting $n$ elements into an empty linked list, if the linked list needs to be maintained in sorted order?

solutionDiagram.alt: Six rows show a sorted list growing as the keys 1 to 6 arrive in increasing order; row k has k minus 1 comparisons, so the total is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15, which grows as n squared.

steps.title: Inserting into a sorted linked list
steps.body: A linked list is a chain of nodes reached from its first node; there is no way to jump to the middle, as there is with an array index. To keep the list sorted, each new element must be placed before the first element larger than it. To find that place you walk from the first node, comparing as you go. Once the place is found, linking the new node in costs a constant number of pointer changes. The worst case means the most expensive input order, summed over all $n$ insertions.

steps.title: Cost of the k-th insertion
steps.body: Before the $k$-th insertion the list holds $k - 1$ elements. If the new element is larger than all of them (for example, the keys arrive in increasing order), the walk passes all $k - 1$ nodes before inserting at the end: $k - 1$ comparisons. No insertion can cost more than that. Binary search does not help, because a linked list cannot jump to its middle node.

steps.title: Add up over the n insertions
steps.body: In the worst case the total is $0 + 1 + 2 + \dots + (n - 1) = n(n-1)/2$, which grows as $n^2$. It is also never more than that, so the worst case is $\Theta(n^2)$. A script tried every arrival order for lists of 1 to 7 elements and found the largest number of comparisons was 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, which is $n(n-1)/2$ for each $n$, reached by the increasing order. The answer is (C).

shortcut.body: One insertion into a sorted linked list costs up to the list length; the lengths run 0, 1, ..., n-1, which sums to about $n^2/2$. A sorted array would offer binary search for the position but pay for shifting, and a linked list has no way to find the position without walking. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Option (A) is the cost of inserting $n$ elements at the head of an unsorted list, or of inserting one element once its position is known. The sorted order forces a search.
Option (B) is the cost of sorting $n$ elements with a comparison sort, or of a balanced tree. A linked list has neither random access nor balancing.
Option (D) is the cost of one insertion once the position is known. The question asks for $n$ insertions, and each one needs a search.

recognize.clues: The structure is a linked list that must stay sorted while n elements arrive, and the question asks for the worst case of the whole sequence. "Linked list" plus "sorted order" points to a position search with no random access.
recognize.contrast: In a sorted array the position can be found by binary search in log time, but shifting then costs linear time. In a linked list the search itself is linear and the relink is constant.

check.body: Count a small case by hand: keys 1, 2, 3 arriving in increasing order. Key 1 goes into an empty list (0 comparisons), key 2 passes 1 (1), key 3 passes 1 and 2 (2): total 3, which equals $3\cdot 2/2$. Arriving as 3, 2, 1 each key goes to the head with 0 comparisons, so increasing order is the worst.

questions.stem:
A queue is implemented using a non-circular singly linked list. The queue has a head pointer and a tail pointer, as shown in the figure. Let $n$ denote the number of nodes in the queue. Let enqueue be implemented by inserting a new node at the head, and dequeue be implemented by deletion of a node from the tail.

Which one of the following is the time complexity of the most time-efficient implementation of enqueue and dequeue, respectively, for this data structure?
questions.figure: A singly linked list of n nodes drawn as boxes with a value cell and a next cell, linked left to right; the next of the last node is NULL. A head pointer points to the first (left) node and a tail pointer points to the last (right) node.

diagram.alt: A non-circular singly linked list drawn left to right with a head pointer under the first node and a tail pointer under the last node, whose next is NULL.

solutionDiagram.alt: Top: enqueue links a new node in front of the old head in two pointer steps. Bottom: dequeue walks three hops from the head to reach the predecessor of the tail in a five-node list, because nodes point only forward.

steps.title: The structure and what each operation must do
steps.body: A singly linked list node holds a value and one pointer, next, to the node after it; the last node's next is NULL (non-circular). The pointer head names the first node and tail names the last. In this queue, enqueue inserts a new node at the head and dequeue deletes the node at the tail. Time complexity counts how many pointer steps an operation needs as the number of nodes $n$ grows. A key fact for the whole problem: you can only move along next pointers, forward, so from any node you can reach the nodes after it but never the one before it.

steps.title: Enqueue at the head is constant time
steps.body: Make the new node point to the old first node (new->next = head) and then move head to the new node (head = new). That is two assignments whatever $n$ is, so enqueue is $\Theta(1)$.

steps.title: Dequeue at the tail needs the node before the tail
steps.body: To delete the last node, the node before it must get next = NULL and tail must move to that node. The tail pointer gives the last node but no way back to its predecessor, since nodes only point forward. The only way to find the predecessor is to start at head and follow $n - 2$ hops. That is $\Theta(n)$, even though tail is available. So dequeue is $\Theta(n)$ and the pair is $\Theta(1)$, $\Theta(n)$: option (B). A script counted the hops needed to reach the predecessor of the last node and got 0, 3, 98 for $n$ = 2, 5, 100, which is $n - 2$.

shortcut.body: Singly linked lists are cheap at the head (insert and delete) and expensive at the tail for deletion, because deleting the tail needs its predecessor. Insert at the head costs $\Theta(1)$, delete at the tail costs $\Theta(n)$. If the roles were swapped (insert at tail, delete at head) both would be $\Theta(1)$ with a tail pointer. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Option (A) believes the tail pointer makes deletion at the tail constant. The tail pointer finds the last node, but deleting it requires changing the predecessor, which is out of reach in a singly linked list.
Option (C) swaps the two costs: it takes the enqueue (new node at the head) for the expensive end and the dequeue for the cheap one.
Option (D) assumes insertion also needs a walk. Inserting at the head needs no walk, because head is a direct pointer.

recognize.clues: A queue built on a singly linked list with head and tail pointers, where enqueue works at the head and dequeue at the tail, and the question asks for the best achievable time. The word "singly" and the phrase "deletion from the tail" are the clues.
recognize.contrast: In a doubly linked list the tail node has a prev pointer, so deleting the last node would be constant time. The singly linked list lacks that pointer, which is the whole difference.

check.body: Substitution for a list of 5 nodes: head to the node before the tail is 3 hops, and for 100 nodes it is 98 hops, so the hops scale with $n$. For enqueue the count is 2 assignments in both cases. Swapping the roles (insert at tail, delete at head) would make both constant, which is the sanity check on which end is the costly one.

questions.stem:
A circular queue has been implemented using a singly linked list where each node consists of a value and a single pointer pointing to the next node. We maintain exactly two external pointers FRONT and REAR pointing to the front node and the rear node of the queue, respectively. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT for such a circular queue, so that insertion and deletion operations can be performed in $O(1)$ time?

I. Next pointer of front node points to the rear node.
II. Next pointer of rear node points to the front node.

solutionDiagram.alt: A circular singly linked queue of four nodes 1, 2, 3, 4: FRONT points at node 1, REAR points at node 4, and the next pointer of node 4 returns to node 1; the next of node 1 points to node 2, not to REAR.

steps.title: A circular linked list as a queue
steps.body: In a singly linked list each node has one pointer, next. In a circular list the last node's next points back to the first node instead of being NULL, so there is no end marker. As a queue, items are added at the rear and removed from the front. FRONT and REAR are two separate pointers kept outside the nodes, one at each end. The question asks which statement about the links must hold for this circular queue to have $O(1)$ insertion and deletion.

steps.title: Statement II is the circular link
steps.body: 'Circular' means the node at the rear links to the node at the front: REAR->next = FRONT. With it, enqueue is: new->next = FRONT; REAR->next = new; REAR = new. Dequeue is: FRONT = FRONT->next; REAR->next = FRONT. Each is a fixed number of assignments, $O(1)$, and the circular link is kept intact. So II is correct.

steps.title: Statement I would limit the queue to two nodes
steps.body: FRONT->next is the node just after the front. It is the rear node only when the queue has one or two nodes. With three or more nodes, FRONT->next is the second node, not the rear. A script built circular lists of 1 to 5 nodes and found FRONT->next equals REAR only for sizes 1 and 2, while REAR->next equals FRONT in every size. So I is false in general, II is true, and the answer is (B), II only.

shortcut.body: 'Circular' defines the last node pointing to the first: that is statement II. Statement I would force at most two nodes. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Option (A) reverses the direction of the circular link: the front node does not point to the rear, the rear points back to the front.
Option (C) accepts statement I because the two ends are 'connected' in a circle. In a singly linked list the connection runs one way only: from rear to front.
Option (D) doubts that a singly linked circular queue can be $O(1)$. It can, because the two external pointers give direct access to both ends.

recognize.clues: The words "circular queue", "singly linked list" and "exactly two external pointers FRONT and REAR" with two statements about next pointers. They ask which link direction closes the ring.
recognize.contrast: A circular doubly linked list has both directions, so both ends point to each other. In a singly linked ring only one direction exists, from the rear back to the front.

check.body: Test on sizes 1 to 5: FRONT->next equals REAR only when the queue has one or two nodes, but REAR->next equals FRONT for every size. A statement that fails for three or more nodes cannot be the property of the structure.

questions.stem:
Consider the C code fragment given below.

Assuming that m and n point to valid NULL-terminated linked lists, invocation of join will
options: append list m to the end of list n for all inputs.
either cause a null pointer dereference or append list m to the end of list n.
cause a null pointer dereference for all inputs.
append list n to the end of list m for all inputs.

solutionDiagram.alt: Top: lists n = 3, 4 and m = 1, 2 where p stops at the last node of n and its next is set to the head of m, giving 3, 4, 1, 2. Bottom: with n equal to NULL the test p->next reads through a NULL pointer.

steps.title: Terms: NULL-terminated list, empty list, dereference
steps.body: A singly linked list is reached through a pointer to its first node, and each node's next points to the following node. A NULL-terminated list is one whose last node has next equal to NULL. The empty list is a valid NULL-terminated list: its head pointer is itself NULL. To dereference a pointer is to read through it, as in p->next, which reads the next field of the node p points to. If p is NULL there is no node, and the read is a null pointer dereference (a crash). So whether join is safe depends on whether n can be NULL.

steps.title: Trace a non-empty n
steps.body: p starts at n. The loop moves p forward while p->next is not NULL, so it stops with p at the last node of n. The last statement p->next = m makes that last node point to the first node of m. List n now continues with all of m: for n = 3, 4 and m = 1, 2, the list from n reads 3, 4, 1, 2. This is 'append list m to the end of list n', and it also works when m is empty, since then the last next becomes NULL again.

steps.title: Trace an empty n, then choose
steps.body: If n is NULL, then p = n is NULL, and the loop test p->next dereferences NULL: a null pointer dereference. The problem says only that the lists are valid, which includes the empty list, so both outcomes can occur depending on the input. Option (A) claims the append happens for all inputs, false for empty n. Option (C) claims a crash for all inputs, false for non-empty n. Option (D) says n is appended to m, but the code links the end of n to m, the opposite. The answer is (B). A script that ran the function on four input pairs appended m in three and raised the dereference error in the one with empty n.

shortcut.body: Read the code for what p->next needs: p must not be NULL. p starts as n, so an empty n crashes, and otherwise the end of n gets m. 'Either, depending on input' is option (B). About 40 seconds. The direction check matters too: the last node of n receives m, so m goes after n.

traps.text: Option (A) forgets that a valid list can be empty. For an empty n the loop test dereferences NULL, so the append does not happen 'for all inputs'.
Option (C) overreacts to the crash case. For any non-empty n the loop stops at the last node and the code works.
Option (D) misreads the direction. The last node of n is made to point to m, so m is appended after n; list m itself is unchanged.

recognize.clues: A short C function that walks to the end of one list, with the stem saying only that both lists are valid NULL-terminated lists. "Valid" does not exclude the empty list, so the input range matters.
recognize.contrast: A guarded version that returns early on an empty first list would be safe for every input. The difference is whether the code tests the head pointer for NULL before it reads through it.

check.body: Run the function on all pairs of list lengths 0 to 3: for every non-empty n the result is the elements of n followed by the elements of m, in order. Only the pairs with n of length 0 fail. That boundary case is the one the options turn on.
